statement.text:
T1: Solenoid and loop
A closed circular loop of radius \(r\) consists of an ideal battery of electromotive force \(\mathcal E\) and a wire of resistance \(R\). A long thin air-core solenoid is aligned with the axis of the loop (\(z\)-axis). Its length is \(\ell\gg r\), cross-sectional area is \(A\) (\(\sqrt A\ll r\)), and the number of turns is \(N\). The solenoid is powered by a constant current \(I\) provided by an ideal current source. The directions of the currents in the solenoid and in the loop are the same (clockwise in the figure).

a
Find the force \(F_1\) acting on the solenoid when its head \(O_1\) is positioned in the loop centre \(O\). What is the force \(F_2\) acting on the solenoid when its tail \(O_2\) is located in the centre of the loop?
b
Suppose now that the solenoid is moving slowly with a constant velocity \(v\) along the \(z\)-axis starting far away from the loop, going past its centre, and proceeding further to the right in the positive \(z\)-direction. Plot the current \(J\) flowing in the loop as a function of time. Highlight important features and values on the graph. The velocity \(v\) is so small that self-inductance of the loop can be neglected.

children.text: a. Solution I: force on the loop

The stationary loop carries current \(J=\mathcal E/R\). Newton's third law gives the force on the solenoid as the opposite of the force on the loop. A long, thin solenoid can be represented externally by a north pole at \(O_1\) and a south pole at \(O_2\). Each pole has flux magnitude equal to the flux through a cross-section of the solenoid.
With \(O_1=O\), the far pole is negligible. The near pole produces an outward radial field of magnitude
Summing \(J\,d\mathbf l\times\mathbf B\) around the loop gives a force in the negative \(z\)-direction. The solenoid experiences the opposite force.
\[F_1=\frac{\mathcal E}{R}\,2\pi r\,B(r)=\frac{\mu_0NIA\mathcal E}{2\ell Rr},\qquad \mathbf F_1=F_1\mathbf e_z,\qquad \mathbf F_2=-F_1\mathbf e_z.\]

When \(O_2=O\), the radial field reverses, hence so does the force. The source also permits a hemisphere construction using half the internal field flux and half the spherical area. It gives the same radial field.
a. Solution II: force on a magnetic pole
The total magnetic moment is \(m=NIA\). Writing this as \(Q_m\ell\) gives the pole strength. The field at the centre of the battery-powered loop follows from the Biot-Savart law.

The north pole is pushed in the positive \(z\)-direction and the south pole in the negative direction. The pole analogy can also be justified by virtual work on the field energy: electric and magnetic energy densities are \(\varepsilon_0E^2/2\) and \(B^2/(2\mu_0)\), respectively. The substitutions \(\varepsilon_0^{-1}\leftrightarrow\mu_0\), \(E\leftrightarrow B\) and \(Q\leftrightarrow Q_m\) give
a. Solution III: flux through the side

The loop field enters the near end of the solenoid with flux \(\Phi_{\rm in}=\mu_0\mathcal E A/(2Rr)\). Almost no flux escapes through the distant end, so it leaves through the side. solution.text:
T1: Solenoid and loop
a. Solution I: force on the loop
The stationary loop carries current \(J=\mathcal E/R\). Newton's third law gives the force on the solenoid as the opposite of the force on the loop. A long, thin solenoid can be represented externally by a north pole at \(O_1\) and a south pole at \(O_2\). Each pole has flux magnitude equal to the flux through a cross-section of the solenoid.
\[\Phi=B_{\rm in}A=\mu_0\frac{NI}{\ell}A.\]
With \(O_1=O\), the far pole is negligible. The near pole produces an outward radial field of magnitude
\[B(r)=\frac{\Phi}{4\pi r^2}=\frac{\mu_0NIA}{4\pi\ell r^2}.\]
Summing \(J\,d\mathbf l\times\mathbf B\) around the loop gives a force in the negative \(z\)-direction. The solenoid experiences the opposite force.
\[F_1=\frac{\mathcal E}{R}\,2\pi r\,B(r)=\frac{\mu_0NIA\mathcal E}{2\ell Rr},\qquad \mathbf F_1=F_1\mathbf e_z,\qquad \mathbf F_2=-F_1\mathbf e_z.\]
When \(O_2=O\), the radial field reverses, hence so does the force. The source also permits a hemisphere construction using half the internal field flux and half the spherical area. It gives the same radial field.
a. Solution II: force on a magnetic pole
The total magnetic moment is \(m=NIA\). Writing this as \(Q_m\ell\) gives the pole strength. The field at the centre of the battery-powered loop follows from the Biot-Savart law.
\[Q_m=\frac{NIA}{\ell}=\frac{\Phi}{\mu_0},\qquad B_{\rm loop}(0)=\frac{\mu_0J}{2r}=\frac{\mu_0\mathcal E}{2Rr},\qquad F_1=Q_mB_{\rm loop}(0).\]
The north pole is pushed in the positive \(z\)-direction and the south pole in the negative direction. The pole analogy can also be justified by virtual work on the field energy: electric and magnetic energy densities are \(\varepsilon_0E^2/2\) and \(B^2/(2\mu_0)\), respectively. The substitutions \(\varepsilon_0^{-1}\leftrightarrow\mu_0\), \(E\leftrightarrow B\) and \(Q\leftrightarrow Q_m\) give
\[F_E=\frac{Q^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0r^2}\quad\longleftrightarrow\quad F_B=\frac{\mu_0Q_m^2}{4\pi r^2},\qquad Q=\varepsilon_0\Psi\quad\longleftrightarrow\quad Q_m=\frac{\Phi}{\mu_0}.\]
a. Solution III: flux through the side
The loop field enters the near end of the solenoid with flux \(\Phi_{\rm in}=\mu_0\mathcal E A/(2Rr)\). Almost no flux escapes through the distant end, so it leaves through the side. For a circular turn with perimeter \(c=2\sqrt{\pi A}\), let \(B_i\) be the radial component at that turn. Its axial force is \(F_i=cIB_i\). Axial field components produce radial forces that cancel by symmetry.
\[F_1=I\frac N\ell\sum_i c\frac\ell N B_i=I\frac N\ell\Phi_{\rm in}=\frac{\mu_0\mathcal E ANI}{2Rr\ell}.\]
a. Solution IV: integrate magnetic dipoles
A short segment has dipole moment \(d\mathbf m=IAN\,dz\,\mathbf e_z/\ell\). Its axial force is \(dm\,dB_{\rm loop}/dz\). Thus
\[B_{\rm loop}(z)=\frac{\mu_0\mathcal E}{2R}\frac{r^2}{(z^2+r^2)^{3/2}},\qquad F_1=\frac{IAN}{\ell}\left[B_{\rm loop}(0)-B_{\rm loop}(-\ell)\right].\]
\[F_1=\frac{\mu_0\mathcal E ANI r^2}{2R\ell}\left[\frac1{r^3}-\frac1{(\ell^2+r^2)^{3/2}}\right]\simeq\frac{\mu_0\mathcal E ANI}{2\ell Rr}.\]
A related construction uses Gauss's law for the magnetic field to obtain the radial flux through each segment from the change in axial field, then integrates the Lorentz force. It gives the same result.
a. Solution V: energy and the sources
Move the solenoid a small distance \(\delta z\) in the positive direction while an external force balances the magnetic force. The system includes its power supplies. The field energy alone is not the total energy.
\[-F_1\delta z=\delta E_{\rm total}=\delta E_{\rm field}+\delta E_{\rm sources}.\]
For this virtual displacement, replace the battery by a source holding \(J=\mathcal E/R\) constant. Only the mutual-inductance term changes.
\[E_{\rm field}=\frac12L_1I^2+\frac12L_2J^2+L_{12}IJ,\qquad \delta E_{\rm field}=IJ\,\delta L_{12}.\]
\[V_{\rm ind}^{\rm loop}=-I\frac{\delta L_{12}}{\delta t},\qquad V_{\rm ind}^{\rm solenoid}=-J\frac{\delta L_{12}}{\delta t},\qquad \delta E_{\rm sources}=-2IJ\,\delta L_{12}.\]
Consequently \(\delta E_{\rm total}=-\delta E_{\rm field}\) and \(F_1\delta z=IJ\,\delta L_{12}\). Moving a segment from the tail to the head changes the linked flux by
\[J\,\delta L_{21}=B_{\rm loop}(0)A\frac N\ell\delta z,\qquad L_{21}=L_{12},\qquad F_1=\frac{\mu_0\mathcal E NAI}{2\ell Rr}.\]
With the tail at the centre, mutual inductance decreases and the force reverses. Without sources, superconducting circuits would conserve flux and their currents would change. Treating their field energy as if both currents were fixed gives the wrong sign.
The field-energy change can alternatively be evaluated by transferring a segment \(\delta z\) from tail to head, with \(\ell\gg\delta z\gg\sqrt A\). The internal solenoid field is \(B_{\rm sol}=\mu_0NI/\ell\), giving
\[\delta E_{\rm field}=\frac{A\delta z}{2\mu_0}\left[(B_{\rm loop}(0)+B_{\rm sol})^2-B_{\rm loop}(0)^2-B_{\rm sol}^2\right].\]
A third version uses the potential energy \(-\mathbf m\cdot\mathbf B\) of the transferred turns. This effective potential already includes the source-energy sign. The solenoid's own field is the same at both ends and cancels, while the distant loop field is negligible.
\[\delta E_{\rm pot}=-\frac{IAN\delta z}{\ell}\frac{\mu_0\mathcal E}{2Rr},\qquad F_1=-\frac{\delta E_{\rm pot}}{\delta z}.\]
b. Current and graph
Take \(t=0\) when the solenoid's centre passes \(O\). Then \(z_1=vt+\ell/2\) and \(z_2=vt-\ell/2\). Negligible self-inductance gives
\[J(t)=\frac{\mathcal E+V_{\rm ind}(t)}{R}.\]
Solution I uses the solid angles subtended by the loop at the two poles. The flux and its time derivative are
\[\Phi_{\rm loop}=\frac{\mu_0NIA}{2\ell}\left[\frac{z_1}{\sqrt{z_1^2+r^2}}-\frac{z_2}{\sqrt{z_2^2+r^2}}\right],\]
\[V_{\rm ind}=-\frac{d\Phi_{\rm loop}}{dt}=-\frac{v\mu_0NIA}{2\ell}\left[\frac{r^2}{(z_1^2+r^2)^{3/2}}-\frac{r^2}{(z_2^2+r^2)^{3/2}}\right].\]
Solution II uses reciprocity, \(L_{12}=L_{21}\). Temporarily hold a test loop current \(J_0\) fixed. Transferring a segment from tail to head gives
\[J_0\,dL_{21}=v\,dt\,\frac{NA}{\ell}\left[B_{\rm loop}(z_1)-B_{\rm loop}(z_2)\right],\qquad V_{\rm ind}=-I\frac{dL_{12}}{dt}.\]
Substituting the loop field gives the same expression. Transcription note: the source's intermediate prose drops the minus sign in \(V_{\rm ind}=I\dot L_{12}\) and labels a flux derivative with the reciprocal indices. The final negative derivative and the plotted current fix the intended sign and convention.
The deviation \(J-\mathcal E/R\) is odd in time. Initially the increasing flux reduces the current. Later the decreasing flux increases it. Far away, the solenoid field behaves as a dipole field, so \(V_{\rm ind}\) decays as \(|t|^{-4}\). Near the centre the deviation is small and approximately linear in \(t\). The dip and peak occur close to \(-\ell/(2v)\) and \(+\ell/(2v)\), with widths of order \(r/v\) and a separation approximately \(\ell/v\).
\[J_{\min}\simeq\frac{\mathcal E}{R}-\frac{v\mu_0NIA}{2Rr\ell},\qquad J_{\max}\simeq\frac{\mathcal E}{R}+\frac{v\mu_0NIA}{2Rr\ell}.\]
These extrema use \(\ell\gg r\), neglecting the other pole. The curve is smooth and locally quadratic about each extremum. The source's summary table abbreviates this quadratic behaviour without writing the nonzero extremal offset. The full formula above supplies that offset.

statement.text:
T2: Mechanical accelerator
A massless thread makes \(N\) turns around a statically fixed cylinder, as shown in the figure. Initially, the free (unwound) ends of the thread are parallel to the axis \(X\). Then, a heavy point-like object \(P\) is attached to one end of the thread while the other end is pulled with a constant velocity \(u\) along \(X\). Find the maximum velocity attained by the heavy object.

The thread is inextensible and flexible. Suppose that the turns of the thread are wound tightly to one another and are placed practically in the same plane, perpendicular to the cylinder axis. Neglect any friction in the system. Do not consider the force of gravity.

Inextensibility fixes \(v_l=-u\).
\[\mathbf v=-u\mathbf e_1+v_\perp\mathbf e_2,\qquad \dot{\mathbf e}_1=\dot\varphi\mathbf e_2,\qquad \dot{\mathbf e}_2=-\dot\varphi\mathbf e_1.\]

The mass rotates around that end at constant relative speed \(2\pi Nu\), because tension does no work in that frame. The laboratory speed is maximal when the relative velocity points in the pulling direction, with the thread perpendicular to \(X\).

solution.text:
T2: Mechanical accelerator

Solution I: rotating basis along the thread
Resolve the velocity into a longitudinal component along the thread and a transverse component. Let \(\mathbf e_1\) point from the cylinder toward \(P\), \(\mathbf e_2\) be perpendicular to it, and \(\varphi\) be the total turning angle measured from the initial thread direction. Inextensibility fixes \(v_l=-u\).
\[\mathbf v=-u\mathbf e_1+v_\perp\mathbf e_2,\qquad \dot{\mathbf e}_1=\dot\varphi\mathbf e_2,\qquad \dot{\mathbf e}_2=-\dot\varphi\mathbf e_1.\]
\[\mathbf a=-v_\perp\dot\varphi\mathbf e_1+(\dot v_\perp-u\dot\varphi)\mathbf e_2.\]
Tension is the only force and acts along the thread, so the perpendicular acceleration vanishes. Starting with zero transverse velocity gives
\[\dot v_\perp=u\dot\varphi,\qquad v_\perp=u\varphi.\]
At complete detachment, the thread has turned through \(2\pi N\). Hence
\[v_\perp=2\pi Nu,\qquad v_{\rm detach}=u\sqrt{1+(2\pi N)^2}.\]
Detachment does not give the maximum laboratory speed. After detachment, use the inertial frame translating with the pulled end at speed \(u\). The mass rotates around that end at constant relative speed \(2\pi Nu\), because tension does no work in that frame. The laboratory speed is maximal when the relative velocity points in the pulling direction, with the thread perpendicular to \(X\).
\[v_{\max}=u+2\pi Nu=u(2\pi N+1).\]
Solution II: a rotating reference frame
Let \(R\) be the cylinder radius and choose a frame rotating at \(\omega=u/R\). The wound thread is at rest in this frame. A point \(Q\) on the pulled end rotates relative to the cylinder with angular velocity \(-\omega\). The mass moves perpendicular to its unwound thread, so tension does no work in this frame. Coriolis force also does no work. Its kinetic-energy gain equals its loss of centrifugal potential energy.
\[\frac12mv_P^2=-\frac12m\omega^2R^2+\frac12m\omega^2r^2=\frac12m\omega^2l_P^2,\qquad v_P=\frac uR l_P,\qquad \omega_P=\frac{v_P}{l_P}=\omega.\]
Here \(r\) is the distance from the cylinder axis to \(P\) and \(l_P\) is its unwound thread length. The ends unwind symmetrically in the rotating frame, so their straight lengths are equal. At detachment,
\[l_P=\pi NR,\qquad v_P=\pi Nu.\]
Adding the rotating-frame velocity to \(\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf r\) gives the laboratory transverse component \(v_\perp=2v_P=2\pi Nu\). Continue in the translating frame after detachment as in Solution I to obtain \(v_{\max}=u(2\pi N+1)\).
Solution III: work and energy
Again \(v_l=-u\). The longitudinal acceleration is \(-v_\perp\dot\varphi\). If \(F\) denotes the signed longitudinal component of the tension, Newton's law and the work-energy theorem give
\[F=-mv_\perp\dot\varphi,\qquad \frac{dE_k}{dt}=Fv_l=mv_\perp\dot\varphi u,\qquad E_k=\frac12m(u^2+v_\perp^2).\]
Differentiating the last expression gives \(\dot v_\perp=u\dot\varphi\). The remainder is identical to Solution I. The signed \(F\) is negative because the actual tension points toward the cylinder, opposite to \(\mathbf e_1\).
The retained solution PDF contains the original partial-credit tables. The automatic field checks the maximum speed, including the motion after detachment.

The plateau at \(\log_{10}I=4.4\) indicates nearly uniform illumination of the spot. Its edge is sharp on the paper but blurred in the photograph, because the camera is focused on the lens, while the spot's image is between the lens and camera.

The second-brightest region, at \(\log_{10}I\simeq3.4\), is paper beside the blur spot, viewed through the lens. Ideally it would be dark because the lens shades it. Reflections and scattering by the glass brighten it. This scattered contribution is much weaker than the brightest plateau. Subtracting \(10^{3.4}\) from \(10^{4.4}\) can refine the estimate. The darkest region, with \(\log_{10}I<1.75\), is the black interior of the lens. The region \(x>420\), with \(\log_{10}I\simeq1.95\), is unobscured white paper.

Let \(k\) be the ratio of the blur-spot area to the lens aperture area. The lens concentrates the received light onto that spot, so its luminance is \(1/k\) times that of the directly illuminated paper. Explanation 1 from the source: a source of fixed area at distance \(a\) sends flux proportional to \(a^{-2}\) into the camera. Its image area is also proportional to \(a^{-2}\). Sensor illuminance, the flux divided by that image area, is independent of \(a\).

Explanation 2: a narrow cone of solid angle \(\omega\) carries flux \(\Phi\) from an area \(S\) on the blur spot. The lens images it onto \(S'=S(d_S/d_0)^2\). Similar triangles give \(\omega/\omega'=(d_S/d_0)^2\). Therefore the image luminance is \(\Phi/(S'\omega')=\Phi/(S\omega)\), equal to the spot luminance.

T3: Cat eyes
Interpret the four brightness regions
The brightest region is the magnified image of the lamp's blur spot on the paper, seen through the lens. The paper lies slightly beyond the focal plane. The plateau at \(\log_{10}I=4.4\) indicates nearly uniform illumination of the spot. Its edge is sharp on the paper but blurred in the photograph, because the camera is focused on the lens, while the spot's image is between the lens and camera.
The second-brightest region, at \(\log_{10}I\simeq3.4\), is paper beside the blur spot, viewed through the lens. Ideally it would be dark because the lens shades it. Reflections and scattering by the glass brighten it. This scattered contribution is much weaker than the brightest plateau. Subtracting \(10^{3.4}\) from \(10^{4.4}\) can refine the estimate. The darkest region, with \(\log_{10}I<1.75\), is the black interior of the lens. The region \(x>420\), with \(\log_{10}I\simeq1.95\), is unobscured white paper.
Luminance and the blur-spot size
Since \(L\gg f\) and the lens-to-paper distance \(d_0\) is of order \(f\), the lamp's illuminance is nearly the same at the lens and paper. Let \(k\) be the ratio of the blur-spot area to the lens aperture area. The lens concentrates the received light onto that spot, so its luminance is \(1/k\) times that of the directly illuminated paper. A paraxial ideal lens preserves luminance, and the camera's sensor illuminance is proportional to source luminance. Thus
\[\frac1k=\frac{I_{\rm bright}}{I_{\rm paper}}\simeq10^{4.4-1.95}\simeq282,\qquad \sqrt k\simeq0.0596.\]
Explanation 1 from the source: a source of fixed area at distance \(a\) sends flux proportional to \(a^{-2}\) into the camera. Its image area is also proportional to \(a^{-2}\). Sensor illuminance, the flux divided by that image area, is independent of \(a\).
Explanation 2: a narrow cone of solid angle \(\omega\) carries flux \(\Phi\) from an area \(S\) on the blur spot. The lens images it onto \(S'=S(d_S/d_0)^2\). Similar triangles give \(\omega/\omega'=(d_S/d_0)^2\). Therefore the image luminance is \(\Phi/(S'\omega')=\Phi/(S\omega)\), equal to the spot luminance.
Find the paper and image distances
Write \(d_S\) for the distance from the lens to the image of the blur spot. Newton's lens formula gives
\[(d_S-f)(d_0-f)=f^2,\qquad d_S=\frac{d_0f}{d_0-f}.\]
Assume initially \(d_0-f\ll f\) and verify this afterward. The lamp image is a distance \(s\) beyond the focal plane, where \(s=f^2/(L-f-d_0)\simeq f^2/L\). Similar triangles give the physical blur-spot diameter \(D_{\rm BS}\) and its image diameter \(D_I\).
\[D_{\rm BS}=\frac{D(d_0-f-s)}{f+s}\simeq D\left(\frac{d_0-f}{f}-\frac fL\right),\qquad D_I=\frac{D_{\rm BS}d_S}{d_0}=\frac{D_{\rm BS}f}{d_0-f}.\]
\[D_I\simeq D\left[1-\frac{f^2}{L(d_0-f)}\right]\simeq\frac{D(L-d_S)}L.\]
Consequently the apparent angular diameters of the lens and spot image are equal: \(D_I/(L-d_S)=D/L\). This is also evident from the source's ray construction. Rays \(SAG\) and \(SBF\) connect the lamp to the edges of the blur spot. The intersection of \(SBF\) with \(FO\) gives image point \(J\), and the other edge gives \(H\). Their angular separation equals that of the aperture. Moving the viewing point from lamp to nearby camera changes these angles negligibly.
The area ratio gives \(\sqrt k=|D_{\rm BS}/D|\). Using the paraxial expressions from the source,
\[\pm\sqrt k=\frac1f\left(d_0-\frac{Lf}{L-f}\right)=\frac{d_0}f-\frac{L}{L-f}.\]
The two branches place the sheet on opposite sides of the lamp image. They give approximately \(d_0/f=1.07\) and \(0.95\). The observed real magnified spot image selects the branch beyond the lamp image, giving \(d_0/f\simeq1.07\) and \(d_S\simeq15.03f\simeq83\,\mathrm{cm}\). This verifies \(d_0-f\ll f\). The \(f/L\) correction should be retained here because it is not negligible relative to \(\sqrt k\).
Infer the lamp-to-camera separation

Similar triangles give \(h'=hd_S/L\), the offset of the spot image above the direction to the lens centre. With angular separation \(\theta=h'/(L-d_S)\) and lens angular diameter \(\theta_L=D/L\),
\[\frac\theta{\theta_L}=\frac{hd_S}{D(L-d_S)},\qquad h=\frac{d_{\rm cr}}{D'}\frac{D(L-d_S)}{d_S}.\]
Here \(d_{\rm cr}\) is the crescent width and \(D'\) the lens aperture diameter in pixels. The graph gives a lens edge near \(x=30\), the midpoint of the blurry edge near \(120\), and the right lens edge near \(240\). Thus \(d_{\rm cr}\simeq90\) pixels and \(D'\simeq210\) pixels, yielding
\[h\simeq80\,\mathrm{mm}.\]
Remark 1: proving equality of angular diameters is not essential if a circle is fitted to the visible edge of the blur-spot image. Its centre then gives \(h'\) directly. Remark 2: one can also measure the crescent on the photograph, but reading pixels from the graph is more accurate.

Alternative construction: image of the camera
The camera sees a small circular area of the paper through the lens. Its diameter \(d\) is nearly independent of the camera aperture. Since lamp and camera are at approximately the same distance from the lens, both the lamp spot and this observable area have diameter \(d=D\sqrt k\). Their centres are separated on the sheet by \(d_0h/(L-d_0)\). Therefore
\[\frac{d_0h/(L-d_0)}{D\sqrt k}=\frac{d_{\rm cr}}{D'},\qquad h=\frac{d_{\rm cr}}{D'}D\sqrt k\frac{L-d_0}{d_0}\simeq80\,\mathrm{mm}.\]
This alternative reduces sensitivity to the approximate \(f/L\) correction. Even taking \(d_0\simeq f\) changes the result by only about 7 percent, according to the source. The numeric answer field accepts the requested 20 percent estimate. The original detailed marking scheme remains in the reference PDF.

solution.text:
1. Ice pellets
a. Frozen mass fraction
With the given assumptions of constant droplet size and constant atmospheric density the drag force leads to a constant velocity \(v\) for the fall of the droplet through the atmosphere.
We can assume that the droplet temperature \(T_d\) above \(h_A\) follows the atmosphere temperature profile (also see below) and remains constant and equal to \(T_0=0\,{}^\circ\mathrm C\) during the melting below that height.
For small temperature differences \(\Delta T=T-T_d\) the heat exchange rate is proportional to this difference \(dQ/dt=\kappa\Delta T\). The factor \(\kappa\) depends on the droplet geometry and its velocity, as well as on the air density. Since these are constant, \(\kappa=\mathrm{const}\).
In the region between \(h_A\) and \(h_B\) the droplet is therefore heated at a rate
\[dQ=\kappa(T-T_0)\,dt=-\kappa(T-T_0)\frac{dh}{v}.\tag{1}\]
The total heat transfer between \(h_A\) and \(h_B\) is
\[Q=\frac{\kappa A}{v}=mL,\tag{2}\]
where \(A=5.0\,\mathrm{km}\,{}^\circ\mathrm C\) is the area between the temperature curve and the height-axis in the region between heights \(h_A\) and \(h_B\). The right hand side equates the heat with the latent heat necessary to completely melt the ice droplet of mass \(m\).
In the region below \(h_B\) the liquid droplet partially freezes again. During this process the temperature is again constant. The mass fraction \(\eta\) of liquid freezing before reaching the ground can again be derived from the area \(A'=4.0\,\mathrm{km}\,{}^\circ\mathrm C\) between the curve and the height-axis.
\[Q'=-\frac{\kappa A'}{v}=-\eta mL.\tag{3}\]
Dividing (3) by (2) gives the mass fraction
\[\eta=\frac{A'}{A}=\frac45=0.80.\tag{4}\]
b. Ground temperature without inversion
If the temperature profile follows the dashed line the droplet will completely melt and the heat transferred from the atmosphere will heat it up. Since the latent heat of melting is much bigger than the specific heat of water times some degrees of temperature variation the temperature of the liquid droplet will closely follow the temperature of the atmosphere eventually. Its temperature at ground level should therefore be close to \(8\,{}^\circ\mathrm C\).
For a better estimate let us introduce a new coordinate \(x\) whose origin is at the height where the droplet is completely molten (somewhat higher than \(h_B\)), and which is oriented downwards. For the change in temperature of the droplet we then have
\[mc_{\rm water}\frac{dT_d}{dt}=mc_{\rm water}v\frac{dT_d}{dx}=\kappa(T-T_d),\tag{5}\]
where the temperature of the atmosphere is given by \(T(x)=T(x=0)+2.0\,{}^\circ\mathrm C\,\mathrm{km}^{-1}x=:T(x=0)+bx\). For the difference \(\Delta T=T-T_d\) between the atmospheric temperature and the droplet temperature we have
\[\frac{d\Delta T}{dx}=b-\frac{dT_d}{dx}=b-\frac{\kappa}{mc_{\rm water}v}\Delta T.\tag{6}\]
This differential equation is solved by
\[\Delta T=bx_0+\mathrm{const}\cdot\exp(-x/x_0),\tag{7}\]
where \(x_0=mc_{\rm water}v/\kappa\). From equation (2) we find \(mv/\kappa=A/L\), such that \(x_0=(c_{\rm water}/L)A\approx0.063\,\mathrm{km}\).
Therefore the exponential factor in the above equation is negligible at ground level (the constant is close to \(4\,{}^\circ\mathrm C\)) and we arrive at a temperature difference between the droplet temperature and the atmospheric temperature at ground level of
\[\Delta T\approx0.13\,{}^\circ\mathrm C,\qquad T_d\approx7.9\,{}^\circ\mathrm C.\tag{8}\]
Another phenomenon, which effectively shifts atmosphere temperature as it is "felt" by the droplet, is due to viscous dissipation. It can be estimated by equating the droplet potential energy loss rate \(mgv\) to thermal power carried away by the circumfluent air \(\kappa\Delta T^*\). This gives \(\Delta T^*\sim mgv/\kappa=gA/L=0.17\,{}^\circ\mathrm C\). If both corrections were taken into account, then the droplet temperature before hitting the ground would again be \(T_d\approx8.0\,{}^\circ\mathrm C\).
Answer convention: the official solution gives approximately 7.9 degrees Celsius with thermal lag alone and 8.0 degrees Celsius with the additional dissipation estimate. The numeric check accepts both within the stated 0.15 degree tolerance. Explain the approximation in your workings.

children.text: A solid, homogeneous spherical ball of mass \(m\) and radius \(R\) is made of insulating material and has charge \(Q\) distributed uniformly throughout its volume. The ball is placed on a large horizontal surface, and set in rolling motion without slipping in such a way that its center starts to move with initial horizontal velocity \(v_0\). There is a uniform magnetic field (flux density) of magnitude \(B\) perpendicular to the surface. The coefficient of static friction is large enough to prevent the ball from slipping on the surface. The moment of inertia of the ball about an axis through its center is \(2mR^2/5\).
Describe the motion of the center of the ball and the shape of its trajectory.
Hint: Depending on your approach you may use the following identity, valid for any three vectors \(\vec a\), \(\vec b\), and \(\vec c\).
\[\vec a\times(\vec b\times\vec c)=\vec b(\vec a\cdot\vec c)-\vec c(\vec a\cdot\vec b).\]

statement.text:

The moment of inertia of the ball about an axis through its center is \(2mR^2/5\).
Describe the motion of the center of the ball and the shape of its trajectory.
Hint: Depending on your approach you may use the following identity, valid for any three vectors \(\vec a\), \(\vec b\), and \(\vec c\).

children.text: The forces acting on the ball are the static frictional force \(\vec F\), the gravitational force, the normal force, and the Lorentz force \(\vec F_L\) caused by the magnetic field. None of these forces perform mechanical work on the ball, so the total kinetic energy of the ball is conserved. Due to the condition of pure rolling, the speed of the center of the ball \(v\) is proportional to the angular speed \(\omega\) of the rolling motion, i.e. the total kinetic energy can be expressed in terms of \(v^2\). As a result, the speed of the center of the ball remains constant, but the direction of velocity may change.
The net Lorentz force acting on the ball can be expressed with the help of the velocity of the center of the ball \(\vec v\):
This can be proven by summing up the magnetic forces acting on the small pieces of the ball.

Let us denote the charge of the ith small piece by \(\Delta Q_i\), the position vector directed from the center of the ball to the small piece by \(\vec x_i\). The velocity of this small piece is given by \(\vec v_i=\vec v+\vec\omega\times\vec x_i\), so the net Lorentz force can be written as
\[\vec F_L=\sum_i\Delta Q_i\vec v_i\times\vec B=\sum_i\Delta Q_i\vec v\times\vec B+\sum_i\Delta Q_i(\vec\omega\times\vec x_i)\times\vec B.\]

The second sum gives zero, because terms containing \(\vec x_i\) and \(-\vec x_i\) cancel each other pairwise. From the first sum \(\vec v\times\vec B\) can be taken out, so at the end the net force is the same as the Lorentz force acting on a point charge moving with the velocity of center of mass.

The speed of the center of the ball does not change, i.e. the net force (which is horizontal) should be perpendicular to the velocity \(\vec v\) of the center. Since the Lorentz force is always perpendicular to \(\vec v\), so should be the static frictional force \(\vec F\), as well. The magnitude of \(\vec F\) cannot depend on the position, only on the speed of the ball, so \(|\vec F|\) must remain constant during the motion. As a result, the net force (i.e. the acceleration of the center of the ball) is constant in magnitude, so the ball's center will perform a uniform circular motion with speed \(|\vec v|=v_0\) (see the Figure).

solution.text:
2. Motion of a charged ball
The forces acting on the ball are the static frictional force \(\vec F\), the gravitational force, the normal force, and the Lorentz force \(\vec F_L\) caused by the magnetic field. None of these forces perform mechanical work on the ball, so the total kinetic energy of the ball is conserved. Due to the condition of pure rolling, the speed of the center of the ball \(v\) is proportional to the angular speed \(\omega\) of the rolling motion, i.e. the total kinetic energy can be expressed in terms of \(v^2\). As a result, the speed of the center of the ball remains constant, but the direction of velocity may change.
The net Lorentz force acting on the ball can be expressed with the help of the velocity of the center of the ball \(\vec v\):
\[\vec F_L=Q\vec v\times\vec B.\tag{1}\]
This can be proven by summing up the magnetic forces acting on the small pieces of the ball.
Proof 1. Net Lorentz force
Let us denote the charge of the ith small piece by \(\Delta Q_i\), the position vector directed from the center of the ball to the small piece by \(\vec x_i\). The velocity of this small piece is given by \(\vec v_i=\vec v+\vec\omega\times\vec x_i\), so the net Lorentz force can be written as
\[\vec F_L=\sum_i\Delta Q_i\vec v_i\times\vec B=\sum_i\Delta Q_i\vec v\times\vec B+\sum_i\Delta Q_i(\vec\omega\times\vec x_i)\times\vec B.\]
The second sum gives zero, because terms containing \(\vec x_i\) and \(-\vec x_i\) cancel each other pairwise. From the first sum \(\vec v\times\vec B\) can be taken out, so at the end the net force is the same as the Lorentz force acting on a point charge moving with the velocity of center of mass.
The speed of the center of the ball does not change, i.e. the net force (which is horizontal) should be perpendicular to the velocity \(\vec v\) of the center. Since the Lorentz force is always perpendicular to \(\vec v\), so should be the static frictional force \(\vec F\), as well. The magnitude of \(\vec F\) cannot depend on the position, only on the speed of the ball, so \(|\vec F|\) must remain constant during the motion. As a result, the net force (i.e. the acceleration of the center of the ball) is constant in magnitude, so the ball's center will perform a uniform circular motion with speed \(|\vec v|=v_0\) (see the Figure).

Now we can write down the equation of motion of the ball. The acceleration of the center of mass is horizontal, which is caused by the static frictional force and the net Lorentz force, so with the help of equation (1) Newton's 2nd law in the radial direction can be written as
\[QvB-F=mr\Omega^2,\tag{2}\]
where \(r\) is the radius of the circular trajectory of the center of mass and \(\Omega\) is the angular speed of the circular motion. We can obtain a relationship between the two angular speeds from the condition of pure rolling:
\[v_0=R\omega=r\Omega.\tag{3}\]
The magnetic field also exerts a net torque on the charged ball. The torque is given by
\[\vec\tau_L=\frac{Q}{2m}\vec L\times\vec B,\]
where \(\vec L\) is the angular momentum of the ball with respect to the center.
Proof 2. Magnetic torque
As the ball rolls on the surface, moving charges form loop currents which represent a net magnetic moment. A small piece of charge \(\Delta Q_i\) corresponds to current \(I_i=|\vec\omega|\Delta Q_i/(2\pi)\), so the contribution of this piece to the net magnetic moment \(\vec\mu\) has magnitude \(I_i\pi x_{i,\perp}^2\), where \(x_{i,\perp}\) is the distance of the small piece from the rotation axis of the ball. The direction of the net magnetic moment is parallel with the vector \(\vec\omega\), and its magnitude can be written as the sum
\[\vec\mu=\frac12\vec\omega\sum_i\Delta Q_i x_{i,\perp}^2.\]
Here we don't need to evaluate the sum (integral), if we use the analogy with the moment of inertia:
\[\sum_i\Delta m_i x_{i,\perp}^2=\frac25mR^2\quad\longrightarrow\quad\sum_i\Delta Q_i x_{i,\perp}^2=\frac25QR^2.\]
So the net magnetic torque acting on the ball (in the form of couples) is given by
\[\vec\tau_L=\vec\mu\times\vec B=\frac15QR^2\vec\omega\times\vec B=\frac{Q}{2m}\vec L\times\vec B.\]
The angular acceleration of the ball is caused by the frictional torque and the magnetic torque. As it can be seen from the Figure, both torques have the same direction, which is perpendicular to the ball's angular velocity. As a result, the axis of rotation of the ball precesses in the horizontal plane. To satisfy the condition of pure rolling, the angular speed of the precession must be \(\Omega\). During precession the rate of change of the angular momentum is given by \(|\vec L|\Omega\), so the equation of rotational motion for the center of the ball is
\[\underbrace{\frac15QR^2\omega B}_{|\vec\tau_L|}+RF=\underbrace{\frac25mR^2\omega}_{|\vec L|}\Omega.\tag{4}\]
From equations (2), (3) and (4) the radius and the angular velocity of the circular motion can be expressed:
\[r=\frac76\frac{mv_0}{QB},\qquad\Omega=\frac67\frac{QB}{m}.\]
Answer convention: the scalar radius and angular-speed fields use positive Q for the magnitude of the charge. Reversing the sign of the charge reverses the circulation direction. The qualitative description is for self-review.

The points at the envelope separate the points for which the solution to this equation does exist from the points for which the solution does not exist, hence for the envelope points the discriminant of the equation must be zero,

What we got is a parabola, and the position of the focus can be deduced from this formula. Alternatively, the position of the focus can be deduced from the fact that light rays parallel to the axis of a parabola converge after reflection from the parabolic shape into its focus. Indeed, the touching point of the envelope with a trajectory of a ball launched at \(\alpha=45^\circ\) must lie at \(y=0\) as this launching angle is known to provide the longest flight distance. Hence, the envelope and the x-axis meet at \(45^\circ\), so that a vertical beam hitting the envelope at \(y=0\) is reflected by the envelope into a horizontal line. The focus must lie on that reflected beam, i.e. at \(y=0\).

The parabolic trajectory of each water parcel must touch the envelope (1 pt). Using the knowledge that the launching angles of the water parcels were never less than \(45^\circ\), we conclude that the touching point must lie at \(y\ge0\) (1 pt). This can be seen from the fact that a parcel launched at \(45^\circ\) will meet the envelope at \(y=0\), and increasing the launching angle will raise the touching point.

There are many ways of proving it more rigorously. For instance, one can use the fact (proved below) that the launching velocity and the tangent to the envelope at the point \(A\) where the trajectory and the envelope meet are perpendicular to each other: with \(\alpha+\beta=90^\circ\) (\(\beta\) denotes the angle between the tangent to the horizon) we conclude that increasing \(\alpha\) means decreasing \(\beta\), which is to say that the touching point \(A\) gets higher.

To prove the equality \(\alpha+\beta=90^\circ\), let a vertical light beam be reflected from the trajectory at \(A\): it will go through the focus of the trajectory which means that if we continue it through the focus and let it be reflected a second time from the same trajectory, it will propagate vertically down. The trajectory and the envelope are tangent at \(A\), so the first reflection was also a reflection from the envelope and the reflected beam must go through the focus of the envelope, i.e. the launching point \(O\). Point \(O\) lies on the trajectory, so the second reflection point must be \(O\). As a result of the two reflections, the beam was diverted by \(180^\circ\) which means that the double sum of the incidence angles must have been \(180^\circ\), and hence \(2\alpha+2\beta=180^\circ\).
Locating the envelope on the plotted stream

The water parcels close to the origin are clearly yet to reach the envelope, and those parcels below the ground level have clearly passed the point where they touched the envelope. Since the parcels form a continuous curve, there must be at least one point \(P\) which is exactly at the envelope (1 pt).

There are two ways of finding the position of the point \(P\). The first approach is as follows. Notice that at \(P\), the water curve is tangent to the envelope (1 pt). Hence, a vertical line drawn through \(P\) will be reflected by the water curve so that it will go through the focus \(O\) (1 pt). So, we need to find by trial and error such a point \(P\) on the upper segment of the water curve that the line \(OP\) and a vertical line drawn through \(P\) will form equal angles with the water curve at \(P\) (finding the position of \(P\) with a reasonable accuracy: 1 pt), see the figure below.

Alternatively, we can use the fact that for any point on a parabola, its distance from the focus plus its distance from a horizontal line is constant. So, for an arbitrary point \(Q=(x,y)\) on the envelope, \(y+\sqrt{x^2+y^2}=2H\), where \(H\) is a constant, and for any point beneath it, \(y+\sqrt{x^2+y^2}<2H\). Hence, among all the points at the water curve, the point \(P\) has the largest value of \(y+\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\) (2 pts). We can evaluate \(y+\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\) for a series of points at the water curve and find the one with the largest value (finding the position of \(P\) with a reasonable accuracy: 1 pt).

solution.text:
1. Three balls
Let the ball \(A\) be given an initial velocity \(v\) along the axis \(Y\), which is perpendicular to the rod. The total momentum of the system is conserved, therefore the centre of mass (CM) of the system moves with a constant velocity
\[v_{\mathrm{CM}}=\frac{mv}{3m}=\frac v3\]
along \(Y\). In what follows, we will work in the CM frame of reference, which is an inertial system of reference. Therefore, in the CM frame the laws of conservation of energy, momentum, and angular momentum hold true. The initial velocities of the three balls along \(Y\) are
\[v_A=\frac{2v}{3},\qquad v_B=v_C=-\frac v3.\]
Correspondingly, the total kinetic energy of the balls is
\[E=\frac{mv^2}{2}\left(\frac49+\frac19+\frac19\right)=\frac{mv^2}{3}\]
and the total angular momentum with respect to the CM equals
\[L=m\frac{2v}{3}\ell-m\frac v3(-\ell)=mv\ell.\]
At any moment the three balls form an isosceles triangle with an angle \(2\varphi\) at the top vertex. The distance between \(A\) and \(C\) is minimal when either \(\varphi=0\), or \(\dot\varphi=0\). For \(\varphi=0\), however, the laws of conservation are not consistent with the rigidity of the rods. Therefore, at the minimal distance \(\dot\varphi=0\), and in this particular instance the system behaves as a rigid body whose moment of inertia with respect to the CM can be obtained through
\[I=\frac{L^2}{2E}=\frac32m\ell^2.\tag{1}\]
On the other hand, the moment of inertia \(I\) could be found independently from geometric considerations. Although \(I\) could be found using the distances from the balls to the CM (the triangle's median centre), it is more convenient to use the following formula for the moment of inertia of a collection of point masses with respect to the CM, as printed in the source
\[I=\frac{\sum_{i,j}m_i m_j(\mathbf r_i-\mathbf r_j)^2}{\sum_i m_i}.\]
In our case
\[I=\frac{m^2}{3m}(AB^2+BC^2+AC^2)=\frac m3(2\ell^2+d^2).\tag{2}\]
From (1) and (2), we obtain the minimal distance
\[d=\ell\sqrt{\frac52}\approx1.58\ell.\]
Transcription note: the source's double-sum notation needs each unordered pair to be counted once. The explicit three-pair calculation (2) fixes the intended convention.

2. Solenoid
Magnetic field gives rise to magnetization of water molecules, i.e. each of the molecules becomes a magnetic dipole. An inhomogeneous magnetic field exerts a force on a magnetic dipole. Water molecules, being diamagnetic, are pushed away from the region of stronger magnetic field. Water reaches a state of mechanical equilibrium where the magnetic force is balanced by a force due to the pressure gradient. Hence, in mechanical equilibrium, regions with stronger magnetic field correspond to smaller pressures. When the current in the solenoid is increased, the pressure differences grow, and at a certain moment, a region will appear where the pressure is smaller than the saturation pressure of the water vapour. This is the moment when water starts boiling.
To begin with, let us discuss possible reasonable approximations. First, we can neglect the water-column pressure, which is only 2 to 4 percent of atmospheric pressure. Second, the saturation pressure of water vapour under normal conditions is also much smaller than atmospheric pressure and therefore can be neglected. Thus boiling starts when the pressure drop due to the magnetic field becomes equal to \(p_0\).
We need to relate the pressure difference caused by the magnetic field to the magnetic-field strength. If a region with magnetic field \(B\) is filled with water, the magnetic-field energy density is \(B^2/(2\mu_r\mu_0)\). If there is no water, the energy density is \(B^2/(2\mu_0)\). We can ascribe the energy-density difference
\[\Delta w=(\mu_r^{-1}-1)B^2/(2\mu_0)\]
to the interaction of water and magnetic field. Consider the following thought experiment. We push away a small volume \(V\) of water from the neighbourhood of a point \(P\) where the magnetic-field strength is \(B\). The displaced water fills a narrow layer at the top of the water surface of equal volume. Assuming the magnetic field is negligibly small at the top, the total interaction energy is reduced by \(V(\mu_r^{-1}-1)B^2/(2\mu_0)\). When pushing away water from \(P\), we perform mechanical work \(pV\), where \(p\) is the pressure at \(P\). At the upper surface, the moving interface performs mechanical work \(p_0V\), so the net work performed by water is \(V(p_0-p)\). Energy conservation gives
\[V(\mu_r^{-1}-1)\frac{B^2}{2\mu_0}=V(p_0-p),\qquad p_0=p+(\mu_r^{-1}-1)\frac{B^2}{2\mu_0}.\]
This derivation is analogous to that of Bernoulli's law. The equality can be interpreted as a modified Bernoulli law for zero speed where the gravitational potential-energy density \(\rho gh\) is replaced by \((\mu_r^{-1}-1)B^2/(2\mu_0)\), the energy density of magnetic interaction. Since \(\mu_r^{-1}-1=-\chi/\mu_r\approx-\chi\),
\[p_0-p=-\frac{\chi B^2}{2\mu_0}.\]
As discussed above, the boiling condition is \(p\approx0\), hence
\[B=\sqrt{-2\mu_0p_0/\chi}.\]
Finally, using the magnetic-field strength inside a long solenoid, \(B=\mu_0IN/\ell\),
\[I=\frac\ell N\sqrt{\frac{2p_0}{-\chi\mu_0}}=4.4\,\mathrm{kA}.\]

Solution - Oscillating rope


A) It is evident from the figure that the curvature of the rope in the fundamental vibration is very small. It infers for a possibility to model the fundamental vibration as a swinging of a rigid uniform rod of length 
\(L\)
 about a pivot point at its end. The moment of inertia of the rod is: 
\[I = \frac{mL^2}{3}\]
 and the distance from the center-of-mass to the pivot point is: 
\[b = L/2\]
 Therefore, the frequency of the fundamental vibration is approximated as: 
\[f_1 = \frac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{\frac{mgb}{I}} = \frac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{\frac{2L}{3g}} \approx 0.61\,\mathrm{Hz}\]
 Correspondingly, the period of the fundamental vibration is: 
\[T_1 = \frac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{\frac{I}{mgb}} = \frac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{\frac{3g}{2L}} \approx 1.6\,\mathrm{s}\]


B) Whatever model for estimating of 
\(f_1\)
 is being used, one may deduce on the basis of dimensionality arguments that the k-th natural frequency of the rope is: 
\[f_k = c_k\sqrt{\frac{g}{L}}\]
 where 
\(c_k\)

\(k\)

\(N\)

Since the node point is at rest (in the small-amplitude approximation), the vibration of the part 
\(NB\)

\[f_2(L) \equiv f_1(L - NA)\]
 Hence one may write: 
\[\frac{f_2(L)}{f_1(L)} = \frac{f_1(L - NA)}{f_1(L)} = \sqrt{\frac{L}{L - NA}}\]
 Since the absolute displacement is much smaller than the length of the rope, the distances could be measured in a vertical direction, to the ceiling, instead along the rope. Therefore, by taking 
\(L = 1\,\mathrm{m}\)

\(NA \approx 0.8\,\mathrm{m}\)

\[\frac{f_2}{f_1} \approx 2.2\]

\(L - N_1A \approx 0.4\,\mathrm{m}\)

\[f_3(L) \equiv f_2(L - NA)\]

\[\frac{f_3(L)}{f_2(L)} = \frac{f_2(L - N_1A)}{f_2(L)} = \sqrt{\frac{L}{L - N_1A}} \approx 1.6\]

\[\frac{f_3}{f_1} = \frac{f_2}{f_1} \times \frac{f_3}{f_2} \approx 3.5\]

\[f_1 : f_2 : f_3 \approx 1 : 2.2 : 3.5\]

solution.text:
Solution - Disk in gas


The initial pressure on the thermal insulating layer is 
\(P_0 = nk_BT_0\)
, where 
\(n\)
 is number density of the gas. It originates from multiplying the flux 
\(j_0 \propto v_{x0}\)
 and momentum that one molecule transfers 
\(p_0 = 2mv_{x0}\)
 (elastic collision), where 
\(v_{x0}\)
 is the normal component of molecule’s velocity, and taking the average 
\((\overline{2v_{x0}^2} \propto T_0)\)
. When applying the same idea to the surface with good thermal contact, we find out that the flux remains the same, although the momentum increases: 
\[p_1 = m(v_{x0} + v_{x1}) \approx mv_{x1},\]
 where 
\(v_{x1}\)
 is the normal velocity component of the molecule flying away from the disk. Thus for pressure 
\(P_1\)
: 
\[\frac{P_1}{P_0} = \frac{\overline{v_{x0}v_{x1}}}{\overline{2v_{x0}^2}} \approx \frac{\sqrt{T_1T_0}}{T_0},\]
 which is correct to some numerical coefficient of the order of one.


The net force acting on the disk: 
\[F = (P_1 - P_0)S \approx Snk_B\sqrt{T_0T_1},\]
 and then the initial acceleration: 
\[a_0 \approx \frac{Snk_B}{M}\sqrt{T_0T_1} = \frac{S\rho k_B}{mM}\sqrt{T_0T_1}.\]


Since 
\(P_1 \gg P_0\)
, the disk will accelerate until its speed becomes of the order of average gas molecules speed. After the velocity 
\(v\)
 of the disc becomes on the order of 
\(v_0 = \sqrt{k_BT_0/m}\)
, the flux of molecules reaching the backside 
\(j(v)\)
 decays faster than exponentially due to the nature of the molecular velocity distribution in the ideal gas (for example, 
\(j(2v_0) \approx 10^{-3}j_0\)
 and 
\(j(3v_0) \approx 10^{-6}j_0\)
). That leads to a proportional decrease in a propelling pressure 
\(P_1\)
. In order to compensate for an initial bias 
\(\sqrt{T_1/T_0} \approx 30\)
, it will take around a factor of one on the velocity of the disk. Therefore the maximum velocity of the disk: 
\[v_\mathrm{max} \approx v_0 = \sqrt{\frac{k_BT_0}{m}}.\]


Here we assumed that the disk will not cool close to 
\(T_0\)
 before it reaches the maximum velocity. Let us show it. The acceleration time is approximately: 
\[t_a \approx \frac{v_\mathrm{max}}{a_0} \approx \frac{M\sqrt{mk_BT_O}}{S\rho k_B\sqrt{T_0T_1}} = \frac{M}{\rho S}\sqrt{\frac{m}{k_BT_1}}\]


Since the power of heat removal 
\(P_{th}\)
 is maximal at the beginning (at zero velocity), we can upper-bound estimate the time for the disk to cool as 
\(t_c = Q/P_{th}\)
, where 
\(Q\)
 is the total heat of the disk. The initial thermal power of heat removal can be estimated as: 
\[P_{th} \approx Sj_0 \times k_BT_1 \approx Snk_B\sqrt{T_0T_1}\sqrt{\frac{k_BT_1}{m}}\]
 and the total heat 
\(Q \approx Nk_BT_1\)
. Given 
\(M \approx Nm\)
, we obtain: 
\[t_c \approx \frac{(M/m)k_BT_1}{Snk_BT_1\sqrt{k_BT_0/m}} = \frac{M}{\rho S}\sqrt{\frac{m}{k_BT_0}}\]
 Finally, 
\(t_a/t_c \approx \sqrt{T_0/T_1} \ll 1\)
, and indeed disk will not cool significantly before it reaches the velocity about 
\(v_0\)
.

\(a\)

• Follow on errors that use dimensionally correct, but wrong, derived inputs are not penalized further


• Follow on errors that use dimensionally incorrect derived inputs are penalized half marks each time the input is used


• Writing a formula incorrectly without showing the derivation and using it as an input is not considered a follow on error, but is instead a non-trivial error with a result of zero marks for that part


• Ambiguous locations, magnitudes, or orientations receive zero marks


• Correctly identifying the locations, magnitudes, or orientations of both of the two image dipoles without clearly specifying why will receive full 1.5 points for recognizing the nature of the problem


• Correctly identifying the locations, magnitudes, or orientations of only one of the image dipoles without clearly specifying why will receive 0.5 points for recognizing the nature of the problem
